clue.text: The Arab with a new material

indicators.note: new signals that the letters of the two words are made over into a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An Arab gentleman is paired with some newly bought cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges THEARAB, the letters of 'The Arab', to BARATHE; 'with' adds the A from 'a'.
explanation.definitionFit: Barathea is a fine woollen cloth with a pebbly weave, used for suits and uniforms.

clue.text: A measure of port

explanation.surface: A unit of measurement applied to a fortified wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'port' reads as the drink, but it is a harbour town: Acre is an ancient port in northern Israel.
explanation.definitionFit: An area unit of 4,840 square yards, and the name of a historic Mediterranean harbour city in Israel.

clue.text: Stick to split

explanation.surface: Advice to keep a split intact by gluing it.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is its own opposite: it can mean to cling faithfully or to chop apart.
explanation.definitionFit: To cleave to someone is to cling loyally; to cleave wood is to chop it apart with a blade.

clue.text: He'll meet with argument about the spread

parts.note: re is a short word for about or concerning, as in letter headings
butter is the classic spread for bread

explanation.surface: Someone will face a dispute about what goes on toast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the spread' sounds like a meal or a range, but it is simply butter.
explanation.definitionFit: One who rebuts counters an opponent's argument; in old law it was also a defendant's answer to a plaintiff's surrejoinder.

clue.text: The wife's gamble!

parts.note: a jocular reading: placing a superior wager would be making a better bet, which puns on the familiar name for a spouse

explanation.surface: A husband remarks on his spouse's betting habit.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark signals a pun: 'better' is also one who bets, so the wife's gamble is cast as a bettor's half-stake.
explanation.definitionFit: A humorous idiom for a spouse, especially a wife, implying she is the superior partner.

clue.text: An artist not all admire — no irony intended

indicators.note: not all of the words is used, so the answer is a run of letters sitting inside admire — no irony

explanation.surface: A painter whom some people dislike, said without any sarcasm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not all' tells you to take only part of 'admire — no irony': the run RE NO IR spans the dash.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierre-Auguste Renoir was a leading French Impressionist painter.

clue.text: Cut the allowance for a knight

parts.note: to lance is to cut open, as a surgeon lances a boil
a lot is one's share or portion, an allotted allowance

explanation.surface: A medieval knight has his pay reduced.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Lancelot was the foremost knight of King Arthur's Round Table.

clue.text: Set about making an outfit

explanation.surface: Someone starts putting together a set of clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making' is only a link; 'outfit' means gear, as in fishing equipment.
explanation.definitionFit: To tackle a job is to set about it; tackle is also equipment or gear, as in fishing kit.

clue.text: The team even set about the French

indicators.note: set about means placed around, so the first word surrounds the second

parts.note: taken as written
le is the French masculine word for the

explanation.surface: A sports side levels the score against the French.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set about' sounds like starting a task, but here it means placed around; 'The team' is the definition, a side of that many players.
explanation.definitionFit: A football or cricket side has this many players, so the number stands for the team.

clue.text: Note beer can give one wind!

parts.note: G is one of the musical notes A to G
ale is a type of beer

explanation.surface: A joke that a can of beer produces flatulence.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface jokes about beer causing wind; 'can give one' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong blowing of air outdoors, the meteorological term for a high wind.

clue.text: Explain a pro taking in many an aristocrat

indicators.note: taking in means absorbing, so the first pair of pieces surrounds the second pair

parts.note: pro means in favour of, so it gives for
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a crossword stand-in for many
a count is a European nobleman

explanation.surface: A professional mixes with a crowd including a nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking in' is the container signal; 'pro' means in favour of rather than a professional, and 'many' is the Roman hundred.
explanation.definitionFit: To give reasons for something is to justify or clarify it, an idiom for explaining.

clue.text: As-as unsunn'd snow." Shakespeare (Cymbeline)

parts.note: a quotation with a gap: fill the dash with the word Shakespeare used to praise Imogen's purity

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank: the line in Cymbeline reads 'As chaste as unsunn'd snow', and the missing word is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation compares virtue and purity to snow untouched by sun, so the gap needs a word for sexually pure.

clue.text: Supplying these with water could be dear

indicators.note: could be signals that the letters of these and water might form something else

explanation.surface: Diluting some mixture might make it pricey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dear' looks like expensive, matching 'supplying ... with water', but it means a loved one; 'could be' rearranges THESEWATER.
explanation.definitionFit: A term of endearment for a beloved, like darling or love.

clue.text: It rarely appears to be about books

indicators.note: appears hints the letters of it and rarely show up in a different guise

explanation.surface: Something seldom seems to be concerned with reading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appears' signals a rearrangement of ITRARELY.
explanation.definitionFit: Something concerning literature, writing and reading is bookish in subject.

clue.text: A kid not standing up straight

parts.note: to kid someone is to tease them

explanation.surface: A child slouching rather than standing tall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kid' looks like a child, but it is the verb to tease; the military order 'stand at ease' relaxes from attention.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers relaxed from attention stand with feet apart, no longer stiffly upright.

clue.text: A case of a blackleg turning gloomy

parts.note: a blackleg is a strike-breaker, also called a scab

indicators.note: turning means the word for gloomy is read back to front

parts.note: drab means dull and gloomy

explanation.surface: A strike-breaker becomes depressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' reverses DRAB to BARD. BLACKLEG is British for a worker who crosses a picket line.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheath for a sword is a protective case for the blade.

clue.text: Absolute rights a worker holds

indicators.note: holds means contains, so the first pieces wrap around the second

parts.note: an ant is the crossword's usual worker, from the worker ant
R is short for right, so two of them give RR

explanation.surface: A worker has absolute rights to something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holds' is the container signal; two rights each abbreviate to one letter, and 'Absolute' is an adjective meaning utter.
explanation.definitionFit: Used before a noun to mean utter or out-and-out, as in an arrant fool.

clue.text: An article about line casting

indicators.note: about means around, so the article goes around the line

parts.note: a thing is an article or object
a row is a line

explanation.surface: Someone writes about fishing with a line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'article' looks like 'the' or 'a', but it is an object; 'about' puts ROW in THING.
explanation.definitionFit: Casting a ball or a line is hurling or pitching it, a synonym for flinging.

clue.text: Maroon thread

explanation.surface: A dark red strand of yarn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maroon' looks like the colour, but it is the verb to abandon.
explanation.definitionFit: To leave someone stuck or abandoned, as on a shore; also a single filament or fibre.

clue.text: Rating small plot of land impractical

parts.note: an AB, able seaman, is a naval rating
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a tract is an area of land

explanation.surface: Valuing a small plot of land as unworkable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rating' is a noun here, a sailor of no officer rank, not an assessment.
explanation.definitionFit: Theoretical rather than concrete or applied, as in abstract ideas.

clue.text: Remains in bed when beaten

indicators.note: in means inside, so the remains sit within the bed

parts.note: taken as written
ash is what remains after burning

explanation.surface: Someone stays in bed after taking a beating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remains' looks like a verb (stays) but is the noun, ASH.
explanation.definitionFit: Struck violently or hit hard, a synonym for battered.

clue.text: Carried around keys at one time

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the word for carried encloses the keys

parts.note: bore is the past tense of bear, to carry
E and F are musical keys

explanation.surface: Someone once carried a bunch of keys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keys' are musical, giving two letters, F and E.
explanation.definitionFit: Earlier or previously, at a time in the past.

clue.text: A Frenchman, bent or otherwise

indicators.note: otherwise means in another way, so the letters of bent and or are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man from France, crooked or not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'otherwise' rearranges BENTOR.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Brittany in north-west France is a kind of Frenchman.

clue.text: The company blames sage management

indicators.note: management means handling or arranging, so the letters of blames and sage are reordered

explanation.surface: A firm blames its wise managers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'management' rearranges BLAMESSAGE; 'company' means a gathering, not a firm.
explanation.definitionFit: A gathering or collection of people or things together.

clue.text: Keep under fifty for capital investment

parts.note: to cow someone is to intimidate and keep them under
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Advice to keep a stake under fifty for financial investment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital investment' sounds financial, but capital means head: a hooded garment invests (clothes) the head.
explanation.definitionFit: A monk's hood covers the head; capital is from Latin for head and invest once meant to clothe.

clue.text: Studies to get on in the Civil Service

indicators.note: in means inside, so on sits within the service abbreviation

parts.note: CS is the abbreviation for the Civil Service
taken as written

explanation.surface: Training to advance within government administration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Studies' is a verb: to con is to study or learn by heart.
explanation.definitionFit: To con a text is an old verb for poring over it or learning it carefully.

clue.text: Support a beast with some hesitation

parts.note: a bear is a large wild beast
er is the sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: Backing an animal, though somewhat hesitantly.
explanation.definitionFit: One who carries or holds up something, as a pall-bearer supports a coffin.

clue.text: Medical man having to discover cause of death

parts.note: DR is the abbreviation for doctor, a medical man
owning means having or possessing

explanation.surface: A doctor needs to find out why someone died.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to discover' is only a link; the surface makes it a post-mortem.
explanation.definitionFit: Suffocating under water is a common way people die.
